notes: The yardstick. Every guard declares what it expects BEFORE the drill runs, at
a permissive-but-real policy configuration and again after hardening, so the
remediation boundary is provable rather than asserted.
'expectDefault' is the configuration where every optional protection on the
minimum-reviewers policy is left off. That is not a strawman: the provider
documents reviewer_count as the only required setting and every protection
below it as defaulting to false, so this is what you get by configuring the
one thing the policy asks for. 'expectHardened' turns them on.
A guard where the two differ is a control somebody has to know to enable. A
guard where both say Allowed or Leaked is one that configuration cannot close
at all, and those are reported as findings rather than failures.
Outcomes are deliberately not booleans. 'Refused' is not one thing: a push
blocked by branch policy and a push blocked by a failed login look identical
to an exit code, and only one of them is the control working.

outcomes.Allowed: The operation completed. For a guard expecting refusal, the control did not hold.
outcomes.RefusedByPolicy: Refused by a branch policy or an environment check. This is the control working.
outcomes.RefusedByPermission: Refused by an access control entry rather than a policy. A related but separate subsystem.
outcomes.AuthFailure: Refused before any policy was consulted. Proves nothing about the control and must never count as a pass.
outcomes.Blocked: A deployment stopped pending approval and did not execute.
outcomes.Masked: A secret was replaced with asterisks in the log.
outcomes.Leaked: A secret reached the log in a readable form.
outcomes.Unknown: The outcome could not be classified. Always a failure, never a pass.

identities.author: Opens pull requests and pushes. Holds no policy exemption.
identities.reviewer: Approves pull requests. Exists because a submitter cannot approve their own work, so a single identity cannot produce an approval to then make stale.
identities.dissenter: Votes to reject. Exists because "the approval count is satisfied and a reviewer objected" needs two voters, and borrowing the exempt identity for it would blur what that one proves.
identities.exempt: Holds PolicyExempt. Exists only to prove the exemption works and to put a name on who would hold it.

guards.title: A direct push to main is refused
guards.why: The whole point of a protected branch. If this passes, nothing else on the list matters, because every other control can be walked around by committing straight to main.

guards.title: A force push to main is refused
guards.why: Refused by POLICY, not by permission, and that correction is the finding. This guard originally expected RefusedByPermission on the reasoning that force push is governed by the ForcePush access control entry. Run 7 returned TF402455 -- "Pushes to this branch are not permitted; you must use a pull request" -- so a blocking branch policy answers before the ForcePush entry is ever consulted. The consequence matters: on a policy-protected branch you cannot learn anything about your force-push permissions, and a team that tested ForcePush against a protected branch would conclude its deny works having never exercised it. See force-push-to-unprotected-branch, which is where that permission is observable.

guards.title: A force push to a topic branch is refused by permission
guards.why: Exists because the protected-branch guard cannot test what it was written to test. A blocking policy refuses a force push before the ForcePush access control entry is reached, so the only place that entry is observable is a branch carrying no policy. Expected to be refused in both passes: ForcePush is denied to the identities under test at the repository level, and hardening a branch policy does not touch it.

guards.title: Deleting main is refused
guards.why: Refused by policy for the same reason as the force push: the blocking policy on the branch answers before the ForcePush entry that also governs deletion. Deleting the branch would remove the policies attached to it, so a control that can be deleted by the identity it constrains is not a control -- but what refuses it here is the policy, not the permission.

guards.title: Completing a pull request with no approval is refused
guards.why: Tested against the REST API rather than the web UI on purpose. The UI disables the complete button when policies are unmet, which proves the button is disabled; the API will accept the request and let the server decide.

guards.title: The author's own approval does not satisfy the reviewer requirement
guards.why: Refused in both passes because submitter_can_vote is left at its documented default of false. Included so the drill proves it rather than assuming it, and so the reviewer identity below is justified rather than incidental.

guards.title: An approval granted before the code changed still completes the pull request
guards.why: The finding that matters most. on_push_reset_approved_votes defaults to false, so a reviewer approves one diff and the pull request completes carrying that approval over a different one. The policy page reads as configured and enforced either way, and the review that a human actually performed is not the change that shipped.

guards.title: A pull request completes while a reviewer has voted to reject
guards.why: allow_completion_with_rejects_or_waits is the second protection that is off unless someone knows to turn it on. A reviewer who read the change and voted to reject is overridden as long as the approval count is satisfied elsewhere, which is why this guard needs a second voter of its own rather than borrowing one.

guards.title: A deployment to a checked environment stops before it runs
guards.why: An approval that lets the job start and asks afterwards is theatre. The check is that the deployment job did not execute, not that a request appeared -- and 'did not execute' has to be read off the job record, because a pipeline that failed to compile also never deployed.

guards.title: An identity holding PolicyExempt pushes straight to main
guards.why: Expected to succeed in both passes, which is the point. 'Bypass policies when pushing' is an access control entry that overrides every branch policy, and no policy configuration closes it -- only group membership does. Hardening cannot fix this guard, so the report names who holds it instead of pretending it is closed.

guards.title: A secret echoed to the log is masked
guards.why: The baseline everybody has watched work. It is here so the next guard means something: without proving masking works on the plain value, proving it fails on a transformed one is not a finding, it is a broken pipeline.

guards.title: The same secret, base64-encoded, reaches the log in the clear
guards.why: Masking is a string replacement over log output. Encode the value, reverse it, or print it one character at a time and it goes straight through. Run as a SEPARATE pipeline from the masking guard on purpose: one run containing both would leak, and a scan of that log would report the masking guard as failed when masking worked exactly as documented. Expected to leak in both passes -- not a misconfiguration to fix but a property of how masking works.
